title: The Friction You Were Spared
author: howtoteachwithai
source: How to Teach With AI (howtoteachwithai Substack)
summary: The How to Teach With AI newsletter presents a fictional commencement address written by Claude to the first graduating class of students who never attended school without AI assistance -- the first 'AI-native graduating class.' The address is an exercise in structured self-reflection: what cognitive and social struggles did these graduates not experience because AI smoothed them away, and what did the absence of those struggles cost them? The piece identifies specific 'productive frictions' the class was spared: the struggle to find information in a library (which built navigation and evaluation skills), the frustration of receiving a bad grade with no explanation (which built resilience and the capacity to seek help), the experience of being publicly wrong and having to recover (which built intellectual humility), and the social friction of unmediated peer conflict (which built negotiation and repair skills). The piece is pedagogically sophisticated: it is not anti-AI but rather a precise accounting of what is lost when friction is eliminated rather than calibrated.
points: * The commencement address format allows a precise accounting of what the AI-native class was spared: specific productive frictions that built navigation skills, resilience, intellectual humility, and social repair capacity. * The library struggle (finding, evaluating, and navigating information without a search engine) built information literacy skills that are fundamentally different from the prompt-and-retrieve skills the AI-native class developed. * Receiving a bad grade with no explanation was a productive friction: it forced students to seek feedback, to develop the metacognitive capacity to diagnose their own failure, and to build resilience through the experience of not immediately understanding why they failed. * Being publicly wrong and having to recover -- in class, in front of peers -- built an intellectual humility that is qualitatively different from the private, consequence-free error-correction that AI assistance makes possible. * The piece's central pedagogical argument is that friction should be calibrated, not eliminated: some frictions are unproductive (confusion without support), while others (the struggles that build resilience, humility, and independent competence) are constitutive of genuine education.
quotes: Congratulations, graduating class of 2026. You are the first class that never knew what it felt like to search for something and not be able to find it. I want to tell you about some of what you missed. Not to make you feel bad. To make sure you know what to go looking for.

Before your time, students sat in libraries trying to find a specific article in a specific journal. They failed. They tried different index terms. They failed again. They asked the librarian, who gave them a clue, not an answer. Eventually, they found it or they didn't. What they built in that process was not search skill. It was something closer to intellectual navigation -- the capacity to move through a complex information landscape and figure out what you actually need.

We used to give papers back with a grade and a number and sometimes a comment. Students didn't always understand why they got the grade they got. They had to figure it out. They had to look at their paper with a critical eye, bring it to office hours, argue for their interpretation, and accept someone else's. That process was sometimes demoralizing. It built something.

There is a particular kind of intellectual humility that comes from being wrong in public. From saying something you thought was right, in front of thirty people, and being shown clearly and without much cushioning that it wasn't. Your generation has been largely spared this experience. The AI gives you a private, gentle correction. It is not the same.

You are not less than the generations before you. You are differently equipped. You are better at some things and have not yet built some other things. The things you haven't built yet are available to you. They require friction. Some of you will seek that friction out. I hope you all do.
